summary: Describes a network management architecture that runs the ISO management services and protocol (CMIS and CMIP) over the Internet protocols. It was meant as an alternative to SNMP, but the approach did not catch on and the RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Two different languages existed for managing network machines. This one used the language from another big standards group, but few people ended up speaking it.

subtitle: A profile for running ISO's management protocol, CMIP, over TCP/IP and OSI networks.

tldr.problem: The IAB wanted a long-term network management system based on the ISO management services and protocol (CMIS and CMIP), usable on both IP-based and OSI-based networks.
tldr.mechanism: The memo is a profile: it picks existing ISO and Internet standards, adds a lightweight presentation protocol for TCP/IP, and fixes options such as association types and application context names so products interoperate.
tldr.outcome: It revises RFC 1095 and is marked Historic.

facts.value: need not accept more than 484 octets

today: RFC 1189 is marked Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1095, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it.

sections.title: Overview and Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1189 defines a network management architecture that uses ISO's CMIS/CMIP (Common Management Information Service and Protocol) in the Internet, so control and monitoring information can pass between a manager and a remote network element. Management using CMIP over TCP/IP is called CMOT. Management using CMIP over OSI protocols is called CMIP.

The memo is the output of the OSI Internet Management Working Group of the IETF, acting on a direction from the IAB in RFC 1052 to address long-term management based on CMIS/CMIP. It is not a standalone spec: it must be read with the ISO standards for ASN.1, ACSE, ROSE, CMIS and CMIP, and uses the SMI and MIB documents (RFC 1065, RFC 1066, RFC 1156).
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a short rule sheet that says which parts of a huge international rule book machines should follow when reporting to a manager.

sections.title: The CMOT and CMIP Protocol Suites
sections.content:
A choice of standards plus the agreements needed to implement them is called a profile. The selection policy here is to use existing ISO and CCITT standards and Internet standards. The ISO ACSE and ROSE protocols support CMIP, and Internet standards provide the transport.

The CMOT suite has seven protocols: ACSE, ROSE, CMIP, the lightweight presentation protocol (LPP, RFC 1085), UDP, TCP and IP. The CMIP suite for OSI networks has six: ACSE, ROSE, CMIP, ISO Presentation, ISO Session and ISO Transport. A CMOT-conformant system must implement ACSE, ROSE, CMIP, LPP and IP, and must support LPP over either UDP or TCP. A CMIP-conformant system must implement ACSE, ROSE, CMIP, Presentation, Session and Transport.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a stack of layers. The top one is the manager's questions, and below it each layer has one job until the message rides on the ordinary internet.

sections.title: Association Types and Negotiation
sections.content:
Managers and managed systems set up an association using ACSE A-ASSOCIATE, and the Application Context Name tells which role the requester plays and what type the association is. There are four types: Event (the managed system sends M-EVENT-REPORTs only), Event/Monitor (adds M-GET by the manager), Monitor/Control (M-GET, M-SET, M-CREATE, M-DELETE and M-ACTION, no events) and Full Mgr/Agent (everything). A system must support at least one type, and may be manager and managed system but not on the same association.

The negotiation rules: a managed system may only request an Event association, and must create one if it has an event to report and none exists. Managing systems may request any type. The responder returns the context it will accept, and may negotiate downward, for example from Full to Monitor/Control. If the context returned differs from the one requested, the manager may proceed or refuse with A-RELEASE. A-ABORT is for invalid negotiation and protocol violations, and can lose pending events or confirmations.
sections.plainLanguage: Before talking, both sides agree what kind of conversation it is: only alerts, alerts plus questions, questions and commands, or everything. The machine being managed can say I will only do a smaller version.

sections.title: Implementer Agreements
sections.content:
The memo defers to the OIW Stable Agreements (sections 18.6.2, 18.6.3 and 18.6.5) and adds a few rules of its own. A system implements only the services needed for the association types it supports. Event time is mandatory for all events and uses 1 millisecond granularity. If only time since boot is known, it may be added to the base time 0001 Jan 1 00:00:00.00, and a year of 0 in GeneralizedTime means no meaningful time is available.

CMIP implementations must support all filter items except subsetOf, supersetOf, nonNullSetIntersection and substrings. The add and remove addenda for M-SET must be supported; the M-CANCEL-GET addenda may be, and their use is negotiated. For CMOT, the LPP may run on TCP or UDP, a UDP implementation need not accept LPP PDUs longer than 484 octets, and the session protocol is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds a few small extra rules, such as every alert must carry a time stamp, and says which optional features may be skipped.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1095
sections.content:
RFC 1189 revises RFC 1095. The tutorial on OSI Management was removed, and may be published as another RFC. The sections on how to interpret requests in the context of Internet MIBs were also removed, since that is now discussed in the OIM-MIB-II draft, and the protocol should work with MIB-I or MIB-II.

The text now rests on the final International Standards ISO 9595/9596 rather than the Draft International Standards. Agreements already accepted by the OIW NMSIG were removed rather than duplicated. Association negotiation was changed to match current agreements, while keeping an Application Context Name identical to RFC 1095's for backward compatibility.

Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a cleaned-up second edition. Parts that were copied elsewhere or turned into a tutorial were cut out, and the rest was updated to the final standard.
